header: Date: 2027-03-04 15:00 UTC; Duration: 55m; Attendees: Samira (AE), Ethan (SE), Maya (Product) - Redwood; Priya (Head ML), Marcus (Platform), Olivia (SRE) - Alopex Retail
summary: Live demo focused on an unusual failure mode Alopex saw in prod: session memory/heap growth when long chat history + high TPS coincided, plus intermittent streaming stalls leading to client timeouts. Redwood team walked through the Console, Optimize suggestions, and runtime fallbacks; discussed dedicated burst and VPC options. Agreed to run a soak with customer prompts and converge on SLAs for timeouts and graceful truncation.
topics: observed heap growth with long conversation histories
console telemetry to detect session erosion
dedicated burst policies vs hosted fallback
transcript:
[00:00] Samira: ok hey everyone thanks for hopping on, um today we wanna reproduce the session heap growth you mentioned and run through our playbook.
[00:18] Priya: yeah thanks, we saw a pattern where after a few hours of midnight sales traffic the session memory for some pods kept climbing and eventually the streaming responses would stall and client timeouts happened.
[00:34] Ethan: when you say streaming stalls, are you seeing partial chunks or full stop?
[00:40] Marcus: partial then stop, like the stream choked and the JS client threw a timeout after 30s, sometimes it recovered after 60s.
[00:53] Maya: okay, that's consistent with prefix cache explosion plus overlapping requests, we'll demo that scenario.
[01:05] Samira: quick background — our runtime does continuous batching and KV cache prefixing, but in these edge workloads the effective KV working set grows and we can hit memory pressure on the serving instance which triggers internal GC spikes.
[01:25] Olivia: can you spell KV cache? our SRE wrote K-V cash in the notes and we laughed about it.
[01:31] (laughter)
[01:34] Ethan: ha, it's K-V cache, like key-value cache. so first I'll show the Console trace for a synthetic session that simulates long history and interleaved high TPS.
[01:50] [Ethan shares screen - Console traces appear]
[02:10] Ethan: notice the red bars here - memory rising per-session, GC pauses at 12:37:40, and then a stream stall event at 12:38:10. The client timed out at 30s.
[02:28] Priya: can you show batching? we thought aggressive batching reduces tokens but increases tail latency.
[02:34] Ethan: right - here's our batching slider in Console (smaller batch sizes reduce tail but raise per-token cost). For this workload we recommend adaptive batching: lower concurrency on long histories and enable small burst windows for short LLM calls.
[02:53] Marcus: what about prefix truncation heuristics? our product needs to keep the last 30 utterances for context.
[03:01] Maya: we have a few options - sliding window by semantic segments, token-budgeted truncation, or pinned messages (system prompts). For retail checkout flows you can pin the cart state and truncate system chatter first.
[03:20] Priya: hmm ok. the tricky part was this only crops up under sustained TPS spikes at midnight. so it's concurrent long-history *and* H-TPS.
[03:33] Samira: understood. we'll recreate a soak with 800-1200 concurrent sessions holding 50-70k token histories and a burst rate of 1k requests/sec.
[03:45] Olivia: what about client timeouts? we set 30s default because the checkout UX can't wait.
[03:50] Ethan: we recommend setting client-side hard timeouts to 25s and implementing streaming health runs: if the server takes longer, the client falls back to a retry route or minimal response mode. Redwood Console can propogate request-level route headers to the app for graceful degradations.
[04:12] Marcus: is there an automatic fallback for model variants? say if the large model is overloaded, do you route to a smaller quantized variant?
[04:19] Maya: yes - Smart routing can fall back to a compatible quantized model or a cached response tier. The tradeoff is quality vs latency, we surface expected hallucination/regression risk in the Optimize suggestions.
[04:35] Priya: about private deployment — we are sensitive to PII, could a V P C deployment avoid the noisy neighbor effects?
[04:42] Samira: VPC + Dedicated capacity gives isolated GPU pools and you can pin rollout policies. We'll walk through Dedicated burst config after the demo.
[04:54] [screen: runtime metrics - throughput, mem, KV hit rate]
[05:10] Ethan: here's an example where KV hit rate drops as session history grows, causing more decoding work and memory churn. You can configure preemptive prefix eviction thresholds to force eviction at 60k tokens.
[05:30] Marcus: does eviction cause abrupt quality drops? some of our flows rely on earlier messages for tone.
[05:36] Maya: semantics-based eviction aims to keep 'important' turns; it's not perfect but we can tie eviction rules to your eval set so we measure delta.
[05:48] Priya: can you show the streaming protocol specifics — where do the stalls occur?
[05:54] Ethan: sure — there are two layers: 1) server-side write stalls from backlog, 2) client-level parse/flush delays. In our trace the backlog forms at the runtime write buffer after the KV cache miss spike.
[06:15] [timestamped logs scrolling]
[06:30] Olivia: do you keep full audit logs for those requests for debugging? we need logs for a SOC2 audit.
[06:36] Samira: yes — audit logs with redaction options; we support KMS and customer-managed keys. We'll include the security doc link in follow-up.
[06:48] Priya: also curious about autoscaling — if memory climbs should we scale vertically or spin new instances?
[06:55] Ethan: autoscaler can add instances but session affinity and KV locality matter; we recommend sticky sessions per user to preserve cache warming. For memory growth a mix of horizontal scale + prefix eviction is safer than vertical scale alone.
[07:15] Marcus: ok demo time please.
[07:20] Ethan: launching a synthetic soak now — configured 1k rps, 900 concurrent sessions, 60k token average history.
[07:30] [Simulated traffic begins; Console spikes visible]
[08:05] Ethan: memory per-instance climbs steadily, you can see GC spikes every ~14 minutes, and at ~08:12 we hit a streaming stall.
[08:18] Priya: that's exactly what we saw. how does Redwood Optimize help detect this earlier?
[08:26] Maya: Optimize provides anomaly detectors: session-erosion alert when per-session mem increases by X% and streaming-drop rate > Y. It also suggests bin-specific batching and quantization profiles to reduce memory footprint.
[08:43] Olivia: can Optimize recommend specific quant levels? we tried q4_0 and saw quality regressions.
[08:50] Maya: we surface expected loss metrics per quant profile. For large histories we often recommend per-layer mixed precision or offload small KV shards to CPU to preserve decoding quality.
[09:05] Marcus: interesting. what about request prioritization - can you prioritize checkout flows over analytics calls during a surge?
[09:12] Ethan: yes — smart routing supports token- or route-prioritization. You can tag high-priority requests and they go to a reserved burst pool. Lower priority requests are routed to lower-cost variants or queued with TTL.
[09:30] Priya: how would queuing interact with client streaming? we'd rather send a minimal fallback than hold the socket.
[09:36] Maya: the pattern is to return an early minimal card and dispatch an async full response to a webhook, or keep a short streaming window and then patch the UI when the full arrives.
[09:48] Samira: here's a concrete playbook: 1) set client hard timeout 25s, 2) reserve a 5% burst pool for checkout routes, 3) enable prefix eviction at 60k tokens + semantic preservation rules, 4) run soak for 2 hours and collect Console traces.
[10:05] Priya: sounds good. any other safety nets?
[10:08] Ethan: we have automatic model fallback after Xs of no-progress on token generation. Also circuit breakers that surface to the app as headers for graceful UX.
[10:20] Marcus: you mentioned KV offload - does that require special infra?
[10:24] Maya: offload can be to ephemeral SSD or remote cache; for Dedicated we can provision NVMe local shard to reduce GC pressure. For hosted we use managed ephemeral storage.
[10:38] Olivia: what about billing during these bursts? we need predictability.
[10:42] Samira: for pilots we can do a capped burst policy and show estimated token economics; Dedicated gives commit-based predictable unit costs. We'll include cost modeling in the follow-up spreadsheet.
[10:55] Priya: ok demo looks convincing. real question — how often do you see this exact combo in your customer base?
[11:02] Ethan: moderately frequent for retail and gaming verticals with long session histories + peak events; we've built several guardrails specifically for it.
[11:12] Priya: one more thing — our legal wants assurance on retention and deletion post-purchase.
[11:18] Samira: retention is configurable per-route, and we support on-demand deletion + audit log of deletion. We'll route security to share the SOC2/ISO docs.
[11:30] [silence while notes are taken]
[11:40] Marcus: small ask — can you attach the exact console trace from this demo so we can annotate with our timeline?
[11:46] Ethan: yes will attach, plus the raw logs from the soak.
[11:50] Samira: to wrap up, we'll run the soak with your prompt set, send the pricing and pilot contract, and schedule the private deployment deep-dive.
[12:00] Priya: thanks all, appreciate the thoroughness.
[12:05] Samira: thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email with links and next-step items.
